definitions.definition: To protect the health of the healthy and to allay the disorders of the sick (Ca Sū 30.26; Su Sū 1.14); the whole tantra aims at the equilibrium of the dhātus (Ca Sū 1.53).

Life is the union of body, senses, mind and self (Ca Sū 1.42), the continuance of consciousness (Sū 30.22); it is happy or unhappy, wholesome or unwholesome (Sū 1.41; 30.24), the wholesome life being defined by ethical and spiritual qualities.

relations.note: life is the conjunction the tripod describes

name: The tripod: mind, self and body

definitions.definition: Mind (sattva), self and body stand together like a tripod; the world rests on their union; that union is the person, the conscious one, the subject-matter of Āyurveda (Ca Sū 1.46-47).

name: Health as the root of the four aims

definitions.definition: Health is the supreme root of dharma, artha, kāma and mokṣa; disease robs it and life (Ca Sū 1.15); life is the means of dharma, wealth and happiness (AHS Sū 1.2).

relations.note: Rasa Śāstra makes the undecaying body itself the condition of liberation

definitions.definition: Āyurveda is eternal because beginningless, because its marks are established by nature (like the heat of fire), and because the nature of things is eternal; its 'origin' means only its being understood and taught (Ca Sū 30.27); Brahmā 'remembered' it (AHS Sū 1.3).

relations.note: parallel to the Mīmāṃsā claim of the Veda's authorless eternity; Caraka grounds it on the nature of things rather than on authorlessness

name: Āyurveda as a limb of the Atharvaveda

definitions.definition: Suśruta calls Āyurveda an upāṅga of the Atharvaveda (Su Sū 1.6); Caraka has the physician declare devotion to the Atharvaveda, which teaches healing by rites and mantras (Ca Sū 30.21).

name: The descent of Āyurveda (Brahmā to the sages)

definitions.definition: Brahmā → Prajāpati (Dakṣa) → the Aśvins → Indra; then (a) Bharadvāja, sent by the assembled sages, learns from Indra and teaches the sages, and Punarvasu Ātreya teaches six disciples (Ca Sū 1.3-40); (b) Indra teaches Dhanvantari, who as Divodāsa of Kāśī teaches Suśruta and others (Su Sū 1.20-21); (c) Indra teaches Ātreya and other sages (AHS Sū 1.3; Bhāvaprakāśa, where Ātreya himself goes to Indra).

name: The two schools: physicians (Ātreya) and surgeons (Dhanvantari)

definitions.definition: Caraka refers surgical and cauterizing procedures to 'the Dhānvantarīyas' (Ca Ci 5.44, 5.63); Suśruta makes surgery the root of the teaching (Su Sū 1.10-18).

name: Caraka as a portion of Śeṣa, identified with Patañjali

definitions.definition: The tradition's account: Caraka is a partial incarnation of the serpent Śeṣa (Bhāvaprakāśa Pūrva 1.57-65); Cakrapāṇi salutes the lord of serpents who removed the faults of mind, speech and body by the Yoga Sūtra, the Mahābhāṣya and Caraka's redaction — one author of all three.

notes: Scholarly account keeps the three authors distinct (labelled in tch:caraka).

name: The threefold Āyurveda: cause, sign, remedy

definitions.definition: The Āyurveda Indra taught is knowledge of cause, sign and remedy, the refuge of the healthy and the sick (Ca Sū 1.24).
Internal medicine, śālākya, surgery, toxicology, the science of spirits, children's medicine, rejuvenation and virilization (Ca Sū 30.28; Su Sū 1.7-8; AHS Sū 1.5).

name: Authority: the Veda, the āptas and the saṃhitās

definitions.definition: The authoritative scripture is the Veda and teachings not contrary to it by examiners approved of the learned (Ca Sū 11.27); the āptas are free of rajas and tamas (11.18); Vāgbhaṭa both calls his text to be applied 'like a mantra, not to be questioned' (Utt 40.81) and asks that what is well said be accepted whoever says it (Utt 40.86-88).

name: The six categories as foundations of medicine

definitions.definition: General, particular, quality, substance, action and inherence, seen by the sages (Ca Sū 1.28-29) and defined (Sū 1.44-52); the nine substances include self, mind, time and directions (Sū 1.48).

relations.note: Vaiśeṣika's six (later seven) categories; Caraka names the same six

name: Increase by the similar, decrease by the dissimilar

definitions.definition: At all times the general causes increase and the particular decrease (Ca Sū 1.44); hence the doṣas are allayed by substances of opposite qualities (Sū 1.59-62) and all dhātus increase by the similar (AHS Sū 1.14).

Vāta, pitta and kapha are the bodily doṣas (Ca Sū 1.57); undisturbed they sustain the body, disturbed destroy it (AHS Sū 1.6-7); they uphold the body as Wind, Sun and Soma the world (Su Sū 21.8), like three pillars (Su Sū 21.3); each five-fold (AHS Sū 12); in their normal state they give strength and long life as the three aims rightly pursued (Ca Sū 12.13).

relations.note: homonym: Nyāya's three faults are passion, aversion, delusion
the bodily doṣas parallel the two mental doṣas

definitions.definition: Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): prāṇa (head; breathing, swallowing; upholds intellect, heart, senses, mind), udāna (chest; speech, effort, memory), vyāna (heart; all movement), samāna (near the fire; digestion) and apāna (pelvis; elimination and birth) (AHS Sū 12.4-9); vāyu 'whose self is prāṇa, udāna, samāna, vyāna and apāna' upholds the body (Ca Sū 12.8).

relations.note: the Upaniṣadic five breaths, here as divisions of the vāta doṣa

definitions.definition: Pācaka (digesting, between stomach and intestine), rañjaka (colouring rasa; liver and spleen in Suśruta, stomach in Vāgbhaṭa), sādhaka (heart; accomplishing intellect and aims), ālocaka (eye), bhrājaka (skin) (Su Sū 21.10; AHS Sū 12.10-14).

Avalambaka (chest; supporting), kledaka (stomach; moistening), bodhaka (tongue; taste), tarpaka (head; nourishing the senses), śleṣaka (joints; binding) (AHS Sū 12.15-18; functions without names in Su Sū 21.14).

Rasa, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, semen (AHS Sū 1.13), each nourishing the next (Su Sū 15.5) and cooked by its own fire into essence and waste (Ca Ci 15.15-16); secondary tissues and wastes arise from them (Ci 15.17-19).
Urine, faeces and sweat and the wastes of each tissue (AHS Sū 1.13; Su Sū 15.5; Ca Ci 15.18-19); the body is rooted in doṣa, dhātu and mala (Su Sū 15.3).

name: The digestive fires (agni)

definitions.definition: Pitta is the body's only fire (Su Sū 21.9); the belly-fire, the five element-fires and the seven tissue-fires (Ca Ci 15.13-15; counted as thirteen by later authors); four states — balanced, irregular, sharp, weak (AHS Sū 1.8); ojas, tejas and the prāṇas depend on agni, 'agni is the root' (Ca Ci 15.3-4).

notes: Ca Ci 15 checked in the local Devanāgarī e-text only.

definitions.definition: Rasa left uncooked through weak fire, vitiated and lodged in the stomach (AHS Sū 13.25); it obstructs the channels and underlies disease; fever arises chiefly in the seat of āma and is treated by digestives (Ca Vi 3.40).

relations.note: āma blocks the channels

name: Ojas

definitions.definition: The supreme essence of the tissues, identical with strength (Su Sū 15.19; AHS Sū 11.37); seated in the heart, pervading the body, whose loss is death (Ca Sū 17.74-75); the 'supreme' ojas in the heart and the ojas carried by the ten great vessels (Ca Sū 30.7-9); three disorders: displacement, vitiation, loss (Su Sū 15.24).

relations.note: Suśruta: ojas is bala (strength)

notes: The terms para/apara ojas are Cakrapāṇi's gloss on Ca Sū 30.7-9 (recalled).

definitions.definition: As many channels as there are embodied kinds of things; thirteen named, with roots and signs of vitiation; for the mind the whole conscious body is the channel (Ca Vi 5.3-7); vitiation is excess flow, obstruction, knotting or wrong course (Vi 5.22).

relations.note: the yogic nāḍīs are channels of breath and energy; Caraka lists nāḍī only as a synonym of srotas

name: The heart as seat of consciousness and ojas

definitions.definition: The heart ('mahat', 'artha') holds consciousness, the self with its qualities, mind and its objects and the supreme ojas, and is the root of the ten great vessels (Ca Sū 30.3-14); the seat of consciousness and abode of ojas (Śārṅgadhara Pūrva 5.49); Bhela places citta in the heart and manas between head and palate.

Life is the union of body and breath (Śārṅgadhara Pūrva 5.52); the breath from the navel touches the heart-lotus, goes out to drink the nectar of the sky and returns to nourish the body and the belly-fire (5.51); the prāṇas reside in ten seats (Ca Sū 29.3).

relations.note: the prāṇa of the Vedic and yogic traditions

definitions.definition: Two lists: temples, the three vital points, throat, blood, semen, ojas and anus (Ca Sū 29.3); head, throat, heart, navel, anus, bladder, ojas, semen, blood and flesh (Ca Śā 7.9).

relations.note: the three great marmas are among the seats

definitions.definition: Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): 107 marmas of five kinds (Su Śā 6.3-4); the three great ones — head, heart, bladder (Ca Sū 29.3). Detailed treatment: U58.

The doṣa predominating at conception — from semen and ovum, season and womb, the mother's diet, the elements — fixes the constitution: vāta-, pitta-, kapha-natured, mixed, or balanced (best) (Ca Sū 7.39-41; Vi 8.95-100; AHS Sū 1.9-10); it does not itself cause disease, as a poison-born worm is not harmed by poison (Su Śā 4.78-79; AHS Sū 1.9).

name: All substances are made of the five elements

definitions.definition: Every substance is pañcabhautika; earthy, watery, fiery, airy and spatial substances have characteristic qualities and actions; nothing is not a medicine when rightly used (Ca Sū 26.10-12).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): space, air, fire, water and earth with their qualities (sound, touch, form, taste, smell), each succeeding one having one more quality (Ca Śā 1.27-28); the person's six dhātus are the five elements and consciousness (Śā 1.16; 5.4); in Suśruta space is rich in sattva, air in rajas, fire in sattva and rajas, water in sattva and tamas, earth in tamas (Su Śā 1.20).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): in Caraka rajas and tamas are the doṣas of mind, sattva its pure state (Sū 1.57; Śā 4.34-36); the person bound by rajas and tamas turns on the wheel of births and is freed by the increase of sattva (Śā 1.36, 1.68); sixteen mental types classified by guṇa (Śā 4.37-40; Su Śā 4.81-98); in Suśruta the unmanifest is marked by the three guṇas and the elements are guṇa-dominant (Su Śā 1.3, 1.20).
Heavy/light, cold/hot, unctuous/dry, slow/sharp, stable/mobile, soft/hard, clear/slimy, smooth/rough, subtle/gross, dense/liquid (Ca Sū 25.36; AHS Sū 1.18).

Sweet, sour, salt, pungent, bitter, astringent (Ca Sū 1.65; 26.9); their source is water; sweet, sour and salt overcome vāta, astringent, sweet and bitter pitta, astringent, pungent and bitter kapha (Sū 1.66).

name: Taste, quality, potency, post-digestive effect and specific power

definitions.definition: The five aspects by which a substance acts: taste, the twenty qualities, potency (hot/cold), vipāka (sweet/sour/pungent) and specific power (AHS Sū 1.14-18; Ca Sū 26).

name: Health as balance of the dhātus

definitions.definition: Disorder is imbalance of the dhātus, balance is the normal state; health is happiness, disorder suffering (Ca Sū 9.4); balance of the dhātus is the effect the tantra seeks (Sū 1.53); health is doṣa-balance (AHS Sū 1.20).
Balanced doṣas, fire, tissues, wastes and functions, with a clear self, senses and mind (Su Sū 15.41).

relations.note: the same state described by its components

name: The two doṣas of the mind (rajas and tamas)

definitions.definition: Rajas and tamas are the doṣas of the mind (Ca Sū 1.57; Śā 4.34; AHS Sū 1.21); they are allayed by knowledge, understanding, steadiness, memory and concentration (Ca Sū 1.58) — 'knowledge of intellect, steadiness and the self' (AHS Sū 1.26).

Beyond the senses; one, atomic; its presence or absence explains knowledge arising or not; it directs the senses, restrains itself, reasons and considers, and then buddhi decides (Ca Sū 8.4-7; Śā 1.18-23); unconscious though active, the self being the conscious agent (Śā 1.75-76); three kinds by guṇa (Śā 3.13; 4.36); located between head and palate, with citta in the heart (Bhela Ci 8).

relations.note: Caraka counts only manas and buddhi here; no fourfold inner organ

definitions.definition: Pure mind sevenfold (like Brahmā, the ṛṣis, Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, Kubera, Gandharvas); rājasa sixfold (asura, rākṣasa, piśāca, serpent, preta, bird); tāmasa threefold (beast, fish, plant) (Ca Śā 4.37-40; Su Śā 4.81-98).
Superior, middling and inferior mind: the superior bear great pain even with small bodies; the inferior cannot be sustained by self or others (Ca Vi 8.119).

The supreme self is changeless, eternal, the seer, cause of consciousness together with mind, elements and senses (Sū 1.56); beginningless, the unmanifest knower of the field, all-pervading yet feeling only through its own senses, witness of all, known by the marks of life, without which the body is an empty house (Śā 1.59-85); the empirical person (rāśi-puruṣa) is born of delusion, desire, aversion and karma (Śā 1.53); the inner self of the embryo is eternal and 'produces itself' (Śā 3.8). Caraka argues against those who teach an ownerless aggregate of momentary things (Śā 1.46-51).

relations.note: Suśruta: selves are eternal but not all-pervading
Caraka rejects the no-self aggregate view

name: The knowers of the field in Suśruta

definitions.definition: Many eternal knowers of the field supported by the one unmanifest (Su Śā 1.3); in Āyurveda they are taught as eternal but not all-pervading, born among animals, men and gods (Su Śā 1.16).

Three accounts: the six dhātus (five elements and consciousness), consciousness alone, or the aggregate of twenty-four (Ca Śā 1.16-17); the conjunction of mind, self and body (Sū 1.46-47); the five elements with the embodied one — the substrate of treatment (Su Sū 1.22).

The aggregate of twenty-four in which action, fruit, knowledge, pleasure and pain rest; born of delusion, desire, aversion and karma; endless while joined with rajas and tamas, ceasing with the increase of sattva (Ca Śā 1.35-38, 1.53).

name: Caraka's and Suśruta's scheme of principles

definitions.definition: Caraka: the eightfold prakṛti (unmanifest, buddhi, ego-sense, five elements) and sixteen modifications (ten senses, mind, five objects); the unmanifest is the knower of the field (Śā 1.61-65); creation and dissolution follow (1.66-69). Suśruta: twenty-four principles and the person as the twenty-fifth (Su Śā 1.3-9).

relations.note: Sāṃkhya's scheme; Caraka merges puruṣa with the unmanifest (24 not 25)

name: The person is the measure of the world

definitions.definition: Whatever is in the world is in the person and vice versa: earth is the person's form, water moisture, fire heat, wind breath, space cavities, brahman the inner self; Prajāpati is mind, Indra ego-sense, the sun intake, Rudra anger, Soma serenity; creation is conception and the four ages childhood, youth, age and disease (Ca Śā 5.3-5); seeing the world in oneself and oneself in the world gives rise to the true understanding that leads to release (Śā 5.7).

name: Sleep in Āyurveda

definitions.definition: Sleep comes when the tired mind and senses withdraw from their objects; happiness, strength, knowledge and life depend on it; seven kinds — from tamas (root of sin), kapha, fatigue, adventitious, disease-following, and from night's nature (the nurse of beings) (Ca Sū 21.35-38, 21.58-59; AHS Sū 7.53-56).

notes: The text names six sources; commentators count seven by dividing fatigue of mind and body.

definitions.definition: Of what was seen, heard, experienced, longed for, imagined, portending (bhāvika), and born of the doṣas (Ca In 5.43).

When the mind is steady and established in the self, pleasure and pain cease and mastery arises — this is yoga, which leads to liberation (Ca Śā 1.137-139); its eight powers arise from concentration of the purified mind (1.141); the path of yoga and of the Sāṃkhyas is the recollection of truth (1.150-151).

relations.note: Patañjali's definition of yoga; Caraka defines it by the cessation of feeling

definitions.definition: Pleasure and pain arise from the fourfold contact of self, sense, mind and object; craving arises from them and grasps their seats; their seat is mind and the sensate body; all feeling ceases in yoga and completely in liberation (Ca Śā 1.130-139).
Grasping sign and form, similarity, contrast, attentiveness, repetition, the yoga of knowledge, hearing again, and (so) recalling the seen, heard and experienced (Ca Śā 1.148-149).

Unwholesome contact of senses and objects, failure of discernment (prajñāparādha) and transformation/time (pariṇāma), each excessive, deficient or wrong; balanced they cause health (Ca Sū 11.37-43; Sū 1.54; AHS Sū 1.19).

The inauspicious act done by one whose intellect, resolve and memory have lapsed; the provoker of all doṣas (Ca Śā 1.98-109); cause of exogenous and mental disease (Sū 7.51-52), of exogenous insanity (Ni 7.10) and, via adharma, of epidemics (Vi 3.20).

relations.note: it provokes all doṣas
through adharma

definitions.definition: Endogenous, exogenous and mental (Ca Sū 11.45); adventitious, bodily, mental and natural — hunger, thirst, old age, death, sleep (Su Sū 1.24-25); curable (easy or difficult) and incurable (palliable or rejectable) (Ca Sū 10.9).

Curable disorders turn back by opposite-quality medicines rightly applied; no remedy is taught for the incurable (Ca Sū 1.62-63); a physician who treats the incurable loses wealth, learning and fame (Sū 10.8).

Resting on the divine (mantra, gems, rites, offerings, vows, pilgrimage), on reasoned application (diet and drugs), and conquest of the mind (Ca Sū 11.54); bodily doṣas by the first two, mental doṣas by knowledge, understanding, steadiness, memory and concentration (Sū 1.58).

Restraining the mind from unwholesome objects (Ca Sū 11.54); for mental illness: attending to the three aims, serving those who know them, and knowing oneself, place, family, time and strength (Sū 11.46-47); 'knowledge of intellect, steadiness, the self' is the best medicine for the mind (AHS Sū 1.26).
Emesis, purgation, decoction enema, oil enema and nasal evacuation, preceded by oleation and sudation; seasonal cleansing prevents disease (Ca Sū 7.46-49; AHS Sū 1.25; 4.25-26). Summary only.
Accumulation, provocation, spreading, lodging, manifestation and differentiation, each a time for treatment; doṣas removed at accumulation do not advance (Su Sū 21.18-37).

name: The five means of knowing disease

definitions.definition: Cause, prodrome, manifest signs, response to trial, pathogenesis (Mādhava Nidāna 1.4; AHS Sū 1.22).

name: The tenfold examination of the patient (and the ten things to be examined)

definitions.definition: The patient is examined by constitution, morbid state, tissue-excellence, compactness, measure, suitability, mind, capacity for food, capacity for exercise and age (Ca Vi 8.94); distinct is the list of ten things to be examined before action — cause, instrument, source and effect, its fruit, continuation, place, time, undertaking, means (Vi 8.84).
The pulse at the root of the thumb as witness of life, with the gaits of the doṣas (Śārṅgadhara Pūrva 3.1-5); a later addition to the classical examinations.
Physician, medicine, attendant and patient, each with four qualities; the physician is chief (Ca Sū 9.3-13; AHS Sū 1.27-29).

name: The conduct and ethics of the physician

definitions.definition: Friendliness, compassion to the afflicted, delight in the curable, equanimity toward the dying (Ca Sū 9.26); to treat out of compassion not profit (Ci 1.4.57-62); a second birth at completion of study (1.4.52-53); the true, the 'reputed' and the pretending physicians (Sū 11.50-53; 29.5-12); never to give an unknown drug (Sū 1.127-130); the student's oath (Vi 8.13).

relations.note: maitrī, karuṇā, prīti/harṣa and upekṣā as the physician's conduct

definitions.definition: The right joining of drug, place, time and person; knowledge of names and forms alone is not enough; an unknown drug is poison, a known one nectar (Ca Sū 1.120-127).
Authoritative testimony, perception, inference and yukti (Ca Sū 11.17-26); for diagnosis three (Vi 4.3); in the debate chapter tradition and analogy also appear among the terms (Vi 8.27).

relations.note: Nyāya counts four with analogy and without yukti

definitions.definition: Thirty-six devices in Caraka (Si 12.41-45) and thirty-two in Suśruta (Utt 65.3) by which a treatise is opened as a lotus by the sun; without them the texts are not understood (Si 12.46-49).
Friendly and hostile discussion, rules of conduct, the forty-four terms of debate, vāda as jalpa or vitaṇḍā (Ca Vi 8.15-28).

relations.note: shared vocabulary (vāda, jalpa, vitaṇḍā) with Nyāya Sūtra 1.2

name: Choosing treatise, teacher and student; initiation

definitions.definition: First examine the treatise, then the teacher (learned, experienced, pure, patient, affectionate); serve him like fire, god, king and father; the teacher examines the student; initiation before fire with an oath of celibacy, truth, non-violence and service of the sick; the whole world is teacher to the wise (Ca Vi 8.3-14).
Food, sleep and continence (brahmacarya) uphold the body as pillars a house (Ca Sū 11.35; AHS Sū 7.52).
Innate, temporal (season and age) and acquired (diet and activity) (Ca Sū 11.36).

Rising at the brāhma muhūrta, cleaning teeth, collyrium, nasal oil, gargling, oil massage, exercise to half strength, bathing, measured food, good conduct and sleep after remembering gods and teachers (AHS Sū 2; Ca Sū 5; Su Ci 24).

Diet and conduct suited to the six seasons and to the 'taking' and 'releasing' halves of the year (Ca Sū 6; AHS Sū 3); doṣas accumulated in one season are to be cleared in the next (Ca Sū 7.46; Śā 2.45).

name: The taking and releasing halves of the year

definitions.definition: In the northern course the sun and wind take away moisture and strength; in the southern course the moon gives it back (Ca Sū 6.4-8; AHS Sū 3.2-7).

Conduct followed with mindfulness that brings health and mastery of the senses; worship, purity, truthful and gentle speech, no taking or coveting what is another's, avoiding bad company; devotion to continence, knowledge, giving, friendliness, compassion, joy, equanimity and calm (Ca Sū 8.17-29); in Vāgbhaṭa, dharma as the condition of happiness, the ten sinful acts abandoned, all beings seen as oneself, the middle way, and constant mindfulness (AHS Sū 2.20-47).

name: The ten sinful acts of body, speech and mind

definitions.definition: Violence, theft, sexual misconduct; slander, harsh speech, falsehood, idle talk; malice, covetousness, wrong view (AHS Sū 2.21-22).

relations.note: identical list to the Buddhist ten unwholesome courses of action

definitions.definition: Rash acts of mind, speech and body; greed, grief, fear, anger, pride, shamelessness, envy, excessive passion and covetousness; harsh, false and untimely speech; acts that harm others (Ca Sū 7.26-29; AHS Sū 4.24) — as against the natural urges that must not be suppressed (Sū 7.3-4).

name: The eight factors of the rule of diet

definitions.definition: Nature, preparation, combination, quantity, place, time, rules of eating, and the eater (Ca Vi 1.21).
What keeps the balanced tissues balanced and restores the unbalanced is wholesome (Ca Sū 25.33); wholesome food alone makes the person grow (25.31).
What agrees by continuous use; changes to be made gradually so that reduced faults do not return (Ca Sū 7.36-38; Vi 8.118).

Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the means to long life, memory, intelligence, health, youth, lustre and strength, the obtaining of excellent tissues (Ca Ci 1.1.7-8; AHS Utt 39.1-2); two modes — entering a hut (better, very hard) and wind-and-sun (Ci 1.1.16; 1.4.27-28); futile in an unpurified body like dye on a dirty cloth (Su Ci 27.4; AHS Utt 39.4) and without purity of mind (Ci 1.4.36-37); lapses are treated apart from it (1.4.29); intellect-promoting rejuvenatives (Ci 1.3.30-31); conduct itself is rasāyana (Ci 1.4.30-35).
Rasa Śāstra: rejuvenation by processed mercury and minerals (Rasaratnākara's Rasāyana-khaṇḍa, 'for the aged'); RESTRICTED — summary only.

relations.note: the Siddha kāya-kaṟpam

definitions.definition: The truthful, non-angry, non-violent, calm, pure, generous, devout, compassionate, balanced and self-controlled person 'enjoys constant rasāyana' and alone gains its full benefits (Ca Ci 1.4.30-35); 'conduct according to the śāstra … is complete rasāyana' (AHS Utt 39.179-181).
The branch that gives potency, offspring and continuity of lineage (Ca Ci 1.1.9-12; Su Sū 1.8). Summary only.

name: The three desires (eṣaṇā)

definitions.definition: For life (first, as abandoning life abandons all), for wealth (by blameless occupations) and for the other world (after establishing rebirth, by the doors of dharma) (Ca Sū 11.3-33).

notes: Contrast (noted, not linked): BĀU 3.5.1 has the knower give up the desires for sons, wealth and worlds; Caraka makes three desires to be pursued.

definitions.definition: Perception is limited (eight causes of non-perception); parental transmission, nature, creation by another and chance fail; rebirth is established by scripture (sages of divine sight), perception (inequalities of birth, untaught infant behaviour, memory of former births), inference (from past karma called daiva) and yukti (no sprout without seed) (Ca Sū 11.6-33); the mind that joins jīva to body carries memory, and with a pure mind one remembers past births (Śā 3.13).

relations.note: Ca Sū 11.8's eight causes of non-perception parallel Sāṃkhyakārikā 7

definitions.definition: Life depends on both: daiva is one's own former deed, puruṣakāra present effort; weak daiva is overcome by effort and weak effort by strong daiva; some karma is fixed in time, some roused by conditions (Ca Vi 3.29-36); karma-born diseases subside only with the exhaustion of karma (Śā 1.116-117).

Death at the exhaustion of life's measure is timely; death midway through wrong conduct, like an axle broken by overload, is untimely; both exist (Ca Vi 3.37-38; Śā 6.28); the life-span of this age is a hundred years (Śā 6.29).

Deviations appearing without cause that show the measure of life and approaching death — in complexion, voice, smell, senses, mind, conduct, dreams — the subject of the Indriyasthāna (Ca In 1.3-7; 5).

Many fall ill at once through vitiated air, water, land and season; the root is adharma, whose source is prajñāparādha — unrighteous rulers, war and curses; remedies are purification, rejuvenation, truth, compassion, giving, worship, good conduct and good company (Ca Vi 3.3-23).

name: The decline of health through the ages

definitions.definition: In the first age men were long-lived and free of disease; from over-eating came heaviness, idleness, hoarding and greed; with each age a quarter of dharma is lost, the qualities of the earth decline and diseases arise; life shortens by a year every hundred years (Ca Vi 3.24-26).

name: The six factors of the embryo

definitions.definition: The embryo arises from the union of mother, father, self, suitability, nourishment and the mind that arises of itself; each contributes specific parts and qualities (Ca Śā 3.3-14).
Nature, the Lord, time, chance, destiny and transformation are held by far-sighted physicians to be the source (Su Śā 1.11).

relations.note: the list of candidate causes in Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.2

definitions.definition: Engagement (pravṛtti), rooted in delusion, desire, aversion and karma and grown into ego-sense, attachment, doubt and wrong means, is suffering and the root of evil; disengagement (nivṛtti) is release, the supreme brahman (Ca Śā 5.8-11).
Beyond treating feelings of the three times, the final cure is freedom from upadhā (grasping), the supreme cause of suffering (Ca Śā 1.94-97).

Separation from all conjunctions through the absence of rajas and tamas and the exhaustion of strong karma — non-return (Śā 1.142); reached by the recollection of truth and the understanding 'this is not I, not mine', after which the self, become brahman, has no mark (1.143-155); disengagement, the tranquil imperishable brahman, called nirvāṇa (Śā 5.11-23).

relations.note: Rasa Śāstra requires an undecaying body for liberation in life

definitions.definition: Entering (other bodies), knowing others' minds, acting at will, divine sight and hearing, memory, radiance and invisibility at will, all from concentration of the purified mind (Ca Śā 1.140-141).

relations.note: the more common list of aṇimā etc.

name: The unprecedented physician

definitions.definition: Vāgbhaṭa's opening homage to the one who destroyed the diseases of passion and the rest that cling to all beings (AHS Sū 1.1), turning the physician's art into an image of the liberator.

notes: The identity of the physician is not stated; readings differ (Buddha, Śiva, the self).

name: Seizing beings and the science of spirits

definitions.definition: Seizure by gods, asuras, gandharvas, yakṣas, ancestors, serpents, rākṣasas and piśācas, shown by superhuman knowledge and action (Su Utt 60.4-7; Su Sū 1.8); for Caraka the seizers strike only one already self-struck by prajñāparādha, and one should hold oneself the agent of one's pleasure and pain (Ca Ni 7.10-22). Summary only.

A Māheśvara system that holds identity with the Supreme Lord yet requires a stable body for the liberation in life accepted by all, and makes mercury the means (SDS Raseśvara 1-5); its end is the vision of the conscious light and brahmanhood here (45-48); mercury is equated with brahman (49-51).

name: Liberation in life in a stable body (Rasa)

definitions.definition: Knowledge of identity with Śiva in an ageless, deathless body (Rasārṇava 1.8); liberation after death is unseen and 'meaningless' (1.9-13); liberation from knowledge, knowledge from practice, practice in a stable body (Rasahṛdaya 1.10); siddhas have attained it in mercurial bodies (SDS 11-12).

relations.note: Advaita's jīvanmukti depends on knowledge, not on bodily immortality

definitions.definition: The body must be made stable before liberation in life; roots and metals are themselves unstable; only mercury stabilizes (Rasahṛdaya 1.10-13; Rasārṇava 1.11, 1.18-20; SDS 1).

name: Mercury and mica as the seeds of Śiva and the Goddess

definitions.definition: Mercury is born of the great union of Śiva and the Goddess, 'the rasa of my body' (Rasārṇava 1.34-36); mica is Gaurī's seed, mercury Hara's; their union destroys death and poverty (SDS 9-10); Maheśvara was born as the great rasa to save the world (RRS 1.22).

The body born of the creation of Hara and Gaurī, permanent though the six-sheathed body is not; those who gain it without abandoning the body are the rasa-siddhas, served by mantras (SDS 7-9; Rasahṛdaya 1.7).

name: Transformation of body and of metal

definitions.definition: Rasa-śāstra's purpose is liberation through transforming the body (dehavedha), not gold-making; metal-transmutation (lohavedha) is to be tested first and then applied to the body (SDS 23-25).
The saṃskāras of mercury to be learned before its use (SDS 18-22; RRS 11.15-16). RESTRICTED: their names and procedures are not recorded here.

name: The impurities of mercury and the danger of impure preparations

definitions.definition: Mercury has natural impurities (poison, fire, dirt) and adventitious 'coverings', twelve in all, each causing disease or death; with them it is poison, freed of them nectar (Rasaratnākara Rasa 1.27-30; RRS 11.20-25); impure minerals and metals likewise destroy life (Rasaratnākara Rasa 5-7; RRS 5.47-48, 5.73).

name: The mercurial liṅga and the worship of mercury

definitions.definition: Seeing, touching, eating, remembering, worshipping and giving mercury bear fruit; worship of the mercurial liṅga surpasses that of all liṅgas (Rasārṇava 1.37-43; RRS 1.23-30; SDS 40-44). RESTRICTED: its making is not recorded.

name: Guru, disciple and secrecy in Rasa Śāstra

definitions.definition: Serve the guru with a pure heart; the tantra is secret and gained by his grace; act only with his permission (Rasārṇava 1.54-59); qualities of teacher and disciple; the unfit gain nothing and lose their wealth (RRS 6.2-10); knowledge only from the guru's mouth and experience (Rasaratnākara Rasa 1.20-22).

name: Mercury and breath: the twofold discipline

definitions.definition: The discipline that stabilizes the body is twofold, mercury and breath; both 'swooned' remove disease, 'dead' revive, 'bound' give sky-going (Rasārṇava 1.18-19; SDS 13-14).

relations.note: HYP 4.26-27 applies the same verse to mercury and mind/breath

definitions.definition: Ādima, Candrasena, Laṅkeśa, Viśārada, Kapālin, Matta, Māṇḍavya, Bhāskara, Śūrasena, Ratnakośa, Śambhu, Sāttvika, Naravāhana, Indrada, Gomukha, Kambali, Vyāḍi, Nāgārjuna, Surānanda, Nāgabodhi, Yaśodhana, Khaṇḍa, Kāpālika, Brahmā, Govinda, Lampaka and Hari (RRS 1.2-5).

relations.note: overlaps (Nāgārjuna, Kambali, Govinda) with the HYP list of siddhas

definitions.definition: Work is done in a safe, righteous land, in a spacious hall with windows and a secluded pavilion (RRS 6.11-14). RESTRICTED: no construction or rites recorded.
